content_html:
Reality as Mathematics

Ideas that “reality is mathematics” range from ancient Pythagoreanism to Tegmark’s MUH. They differ in strength: from metaphorical (harmony of numbers) → ontological (the universe is math). Critics emphasize testability, causal gaps, and the problem of explaining why this particular structure/universe exists.

Theory Core Claim How mathematics relates to reality Representative Figures Critiques
Pythagoreanism
Ancient		 “All is number.” The cosmos is fundamentally numerical harmony. Mathematical ratios and structures are the true essence of things. Pythagoras; later Neo-Pythagoreans. Pre-scientific mysticism; more metaphor than testable claim.
Platonic realism
Classical / Modern		 Mathematical forms exist independently; physical reality instantiates them. Reality is an imperfect “shadow” of ideal mathematical objects. Plato; Gödel; Roger Penrose (to some extent). How do abstract objects “cause” physical reality? Epistemic gap.
Structural realism
Philosophy of Science		 Science reveals structure, not things. Relations are real; objects may not be. Mathematical relations are what persist across scientific revolutions. John Worrall; Ladyman & Ross (“Every Thing Must Go”). Do structures exist without relata? Abstractness vs physicality issue.
Mathematical Universe Hypothesis (MUH)
Contemporary Physics		 The physical world is not just described by math; it is a mathematical structure. All consistent mathematical structures exist as universes; ours is one of them. Max Tegmark. Unfalsifiable? Why this structure and not others? Risk of ontological overload.
Simulation hypothesis
Philosophy / Technology		 Reality is computation running on some substrate. The universe is fundamentally information/algorithms (mathematics-in-action). Nick Bostrom; some computer scientists and futurists. Still presumes a “hardware” outside; regress problem.

References

  1. Tegmark, M. (2008). The mathematical universe. Foundations of Physics, 38(2), 101–150. https://arxiv.org/abs/0704.0646
  2. Worrall, J. (1989). Structural realism: The best of both worlds? Dialectica, 43(1–2), 99–124.
  3. Ladyman, J., & Ross, D. (2007). Every Thing Must Go: Metaphysics Naturalized. Oxford University Press.
  4. SEP. (2016). Structural Realism. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/structural-realism/
  5. SEP. (2009). Plato’s Middle Period Metaphysics and Epistemology. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/platonic/
  6. Bostrom, N. (2003). Are you living in a computer simulation? Philosophical Quarterly, 53(211), 243–255. https://www.simulation-argument.com/
